title: A New World of Gold and Silver
author: John J. TePaske (ed. Kendall Brown)
desc: 86 millones de kilogramos de plata salieron de América en la época colonial. México generó aproximadamente el 45% del bullion total.
tesis: Las cifras duras del saqueo colonial: 86 millones de kilogramos de plata salieron de América, 50 veces más que el oro. México generó el 45% del total, seguido de Perú con 32%. TePaske compiló los datos de producción minera colonial más completos que existen. Los conquistadores primero saquearon el oro ritual de los indígenas y lo fundieron; cuando se acabó, encontraron algo mejor: la plata del subsuelo, inagotable durante tres siglos.
ideas: 86 millones de kilos de plata salieron de América colonial — 50 veces más que el oro.
México produjo el 45% de toda la plata del mundo colonial, seguido de Perú con 32%.
Los conquistadores primero robaron el oro ceremonial indígena; luego pasaron a la extracción sistemática de plata.
contexto: Publicado póstumamente en 2010, editado por Kendall Brown. John J. TePaske (1929-2009) fue profesor de historia latinoamericana en Duke University y dedicó décadas a compilar los registros de producción minera colonial de las Cajas Reales de Nueva España y Perú. Este libro corona su trabajo de toda una vida: la base de datos cuantitativa más completa sobre la producción de oro y plata en la América colonial.

conexiones.razon: Marichal narra la circulación global de la plata que TePaske cuantifica en la fuente.
Galeano cuenta la historia humana detrás de las toneladas de plata que TePaske tabula.

quotes.text: Silver output by weight during the colonial epoch to 1810 amounted to 86,000,000 kilograms, fifty times that of gold. Mexico generated approximately 45 percent of the bullion, followed by Peru with 32 percent and Brazil 14 percent.

The conquistadores apparently took what they could from the indigenous inhabitants, such as ritual plates and ornamental jewelry, and melted them down. When this source was exhausted, the Spaniards found no placers from which to procure gold.

tl: Conquista de Tenochtitlán y primera Caja de México
Mexico City (México), situated on the site of the former Aztec capital of Tenochtitlán, was the only place in New Spain with a royal caja and casa de fundición, and, after 1535, mint facilities.
Pizarro destruye el imperio inca

Cook estimates it at 13,420 pounds of gold (6,100 kilograms) and 26,000 pounds of silver (11,818 kilograms). The gold from Atahualpa's ransom constituted 41 percent of total Peruvian gold from 1531 to 1540.
Fundación de la Casa de Moneda de México

Mexico City became the site of the first Spanish colonial mint, authorized by a royal cédula of Charles V and Juana on 11 May 1535. The order specified that one-half of the coins minted be of one real.
Cerro Rico de Potosí

The most startling find of silver, however, came in April 1545, to the east of Porco at the Cerro Rico (Rich Hill) de Potosí, named Potosí after the Indian word for high places. Potosí became the most productive mining district in the New World.
Fundación de Zacatecas, foco de la plata norteña
Located on the royal road (El Camino Real) about 350 miles northwest of Mexico City, Zacatecas was founded by Spaniards in 1548 as Nuestra Señora de los Remedios de Zacatecas.
Introducción de la amalgamación con mercurio en Nueva España

Introduced in Mexico in the 1550s and in the Andes twenty years later in the 1570s, amalgamation proved especially useful because it more effectively removed impurities from low- or middle-grade ores.
Felipe II eleva a Potosí a Villa Imperial

Philip II issued a royal decree on November 7, 1561, establishing the Imperial City (Villa Imperial) of Potosí. The population of Potosí and its environs may have reached 120,000 inhabitants in 1570 and 150,000 in 1611.
Hallazgo del azogue de Huancavelica
In 1563, they discovered a rich deposit of mercury at what is now Huancavelica, 150 miles south of Lima, a mine worked in pre-Columbian times by the natives for its cinnabar (mercuric sulphide).
Fundación de Manila y nacimiento del comercio global

Students of the flow of American bullion trace the establishment of the world economy to 1571, when the Spaniards founded Manila in the Philippines as a commercial entrepôt where New World silver could be traded for silks and spices.
El virrey Toledo expropia Huancavelica e impone la mita

In 1572, Toledo expropriated the district for the crown, set up a forced labor levy (mita) for the mines, and granted concessions to miners, who agreed to sell the mercury to the royal monopoly at a fixed price.
Apertura de la Casa de Moneda de Potosí
Julio Benavides indicates construction of the Potosí mint began on 8 December 1572 and was completed on 27 September 1575, when it actually began functioning, Historia de la moneda, 16.
Felipe II prohíbe la plata corriente sin ensayar

Such silver had the seal of the caja, casa de fundición, or casa de afinación and the fineness of the silver stamped on it. In November 1591, however, Philip II ordered an end to circulation of plata corriente.
Década pico de Potosí: 69 millones de pesos

In the last decade of the sixteenth century, Potosí yields reached their all-time peak—69,240,000 pesos, almost 98 percent of all Peruvian output and not quite two-thirds of New World yields in those ten years.
Cumbre del siglo XVII: 128 millones de pesos

The general trajectory of early New World silver output consisted of a rise from about 7,550,000 pesos in the 1530s to almost 128,600,000 pesos in the 1630s, a century later, the peak decade in New World silver output.
Crisis del siglo XVII: contrabando y fraude masivo

Nothing exemplifies better the incapacity, even the outright complicity of the seventeenth-century Spanish state apparatus as well as the ingenuity and rapacity of Spanish mine owners, merchants, bureaucrats, religious and naval personnel.
Punto más bajo del bullion novomundano

During the first decade of the eighteenth century, production was 78,250,000 pesos, a low point in New World output since the 1580s. Production rose thereafter to more than 290,000,000 pesos in the last decade of the century.
Traslado del monopolio comercial de Sevilla a Cádiz
Even though the major portion of American bullion exports went first to Sevilla (and after 1717 to Cádiz), much of the treasure was subsequently shipped to other destinations.
Reducción del quinto al diezmo sobre la plata peruana

In Peru in 1736, a royal decree lowered the tax on silver from a fifth (quinto) to a tenth (diezmo), further stimulating Andean output. The decision came in hopes of decreasing production costs and discouraging fraud.
Decreto de Comercio Libre acaba con flotas y galeones
In fact the last convoy of galleons left Panama in 1739 and the last fleet departed Veracruz in 1778. By these dates the sueltos and registros had gradually replaced the convoy system.
Grito de Dolores

Mexican silver output rose, steadily at first from close to 64,690,000 pesos in the 1710s to almost 119,000,000 pesos in the 1750s, but then output increased dramatically until the outbreak of the insurgency for independence in 1810.
Bolívar abole la mita y cierra el ciclo colonial

Additional factors were Viceroy Francisco de Toledo's introduction of the mita in the early 1570s to provide forced labor for Potosí, a system which lasted the entire colonial period until the Liberator Simón Bolívar finally abolished it in 1825.
